summary: Psalm 71 is a prayer from someone threatened by enemies and aware of aging weakness. The speaker asks God for rescue, remembers lifelong reliance on God from youth to old age, and promises public praise. The psalm moves from urgent refuge language to confidence that God’s righteousness, faithfulness, and past help will be told again.
whyItMatters: This chapter shows how Psalms can hold fear, memory, aging, accusation, hope, and praise in one prayer. Near the end of Book II, it gives voice to a person who wants rescue not only for survival, but so that God’s strength can be declared to the next generation.

context.author: This psalm has no author heading in the Hebrew-based text; its speaker is unnamed.
context.audience: Israel’s worshiping and instructed community, and later Jewish and Christian communities that adopted the Psalms for prayer and worship.
context.date: Individual psalms may preserve material from the monarchy through the postexilic period; assigning one date to the whole Psalter would be misleading.
context.setting: The chapter speaks from personal danger, accusation, and old age, but does not name a specific place or historical event.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetic prayer within the Psalter, using parallel lines, repeated appeals, images of refuge, and vows of praise.

outline.heading: Refuge and rescue
outline.note: The speaker takes refuge in Yahweh and asks to be delivered from wicked, unrighteous, and cruel hands.

outline.heading: Lifelong reliance
outline.note: The prayer looks back to youth and birth, naming God as hope, confidence, and strong refuge.

outline.heading: Old age under threat
outline.note: The speaker asks not to be rejected when strength fails, while enemies interpret weakness as abandonment by God.

outline.heading: Praise despite pressure
outline.note: Hope continues as the speaker promises to tell God’s righteousness and asks for time to declare God’s strength to the next generation.

outline.heading: Greatness after trouble
outline.note: The prayer praises God’s unmatched righteousness and expects renewed life, honor, and comfort after many bitter troubles.

outline.heading: Music and final vindication
outline.note: The speaker promises praise with harp, lyre, lips, soul, and tongue, ending with enemies confounded.

keyVerses.text: Be to me a rock of refuge to which I may always go. Give the command to save me, for you are my rock and my fortress.
keyVerses.why: This verse gathers the chapter’s central image: God as a reliable place of safety when the speaker is under threat.

keyVerses.text: Don’t reject me in my old age. Don’t forsake me when my strength fails.
keyVerses.why: The chapter’s danger is sharpened by aging and loss of strength, not only by enemies outside the speaker.

keyVerses.text: Yes, even when I am old and gray-haired, God, don’t forsake me, until I have declared your strength to the next generation, your might to everyone who is to come.
keyVerses.why: This verse connects rescue with witness: the speaker wants continued life in order to tell later generations about God’s strength.

keyVerses.text: My lips shall shout for joy! My soul, which you have redeemed, sings praises to you!
keyVerses.why: The closing praise is personal and embodied, answering the earlier pleas with joy and the language of redemption.

questions.question: Who is speaking in this psalm?
questions.answer: The chapter does not name the speaker. The voice is a first-person sufferer who has trusted God from youth, now faces enemies, and describes being old and gray-haired. In Psalms, an “I” voice can be an individual prayer that later communities also adopt.

questions.question: What does “refuge” mean in this chapter?
questions.answer: “Refuge” is an image for safety and protection. The speaker calls God a place to go, a rock, a fortress, and a strong refuge. The word does not remove the danger; it names where the speaker turns while danger remains present.

questions.question: Why does the speaker mention youth, the womb, and old age?
questions.answer: The psalm frames the speaker’s life as a long history of dependence on God. God has been the speaker’s hope from youth and the one relied on from the womb. That memory becomes the basis for asking not to be forsaken in old age.

questions.question: Are the enemies accusing the speaker of something specific?
questions.answer: The chapter does not state a charge or legal case in detail. It says enemies talk, watch for the speaker’s soul, conspire together, and claim that God has forsaken him. Their speech turns the speaker’s weakness into an argument that no rescue will come.

questions.question: Why does verse 13 ask for accusers to be disappointed, consumed, and covered with disgrace?
questions.answer: The prayer asks for the downfall and shame of those who want to harm the speaker. Their claim that God has forsaken him becomes the reason for an urgent appeal to God to overturn their power. The request to consume them is severe, but it is addressed to God while the speaker is threatened; it does not command readers to take revenge.

questions.question: What does the speaker mean by not knowing salvation’s “full measure”?
questions.answer: Verse 15 says the speaker will tell of God’s righteousness and salvation all day, even while not knowing its full measure. The point is not that praise waits for complete understanding. The speaker knows enough to speak, while admitting that God’s saving work exceeds what can be fully counted or measured.

questions.question: Does verse 20 describe resurrection?
questions.answer: The verse says God has shown “many and bitter troubles,” then says, “you will let me live” and “bring us up again from the depths of the earth.” In the surrounding prayer, the speaker seeks continued life, renewed honor, comfort, and the chance to praise God. That context points to rescue from mortal danger; the psalm does not narrate a death and resurrection or explain an afterlife doctrine.

questions.question: Why are harp and lyre mentioned near the end?
questions.answer: The closing section turns promised praise into musical praise. The speaker says God will be praised with harp and lyre, and then adds lips, soul, and tongue. The instruments fit the Psalms as voiced worship, while the chapter itself keeps the focus on God’s faithfulness and righteousness.

glossary.def: A place of safety. In this psalm it describes God as the one to whom the speaker turns under threat.
God’s right and reliable action, especially as the basis for rescue and the subject of the speaker’s praise.
The speaker’s season of weakness and vulnerability, named as a reason to ask God not to forsake him.
Rescued or bought back from danger; in verse 23 it describes the speaker’s soul as the reason for joyful praise.
